claim: Metal-ion-dependent nucleases play crucial roles in cellular defense and biotechnological applications.
source: Metal-ion-dependent nucleases play crucial roles in cellular defense and biotechnological applications.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of metal-ion-dependent nucleases, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Time-resolved crystallography has resolved catalytic details of metal-ion-dependent DNA hydrolysis and synthesis, uncovering the essential roles of multiple metal ions during catalysis.
source: Time-resolved crystallography has resolved catalytic details of metal-ion-dependent DNA hydrolysis and synthesis, uncovering the essential roles of multiple metal ions during catalysis.
evidence: This statement references prior work using time-resolved crystallography, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The histidine-metal (His-Me) superfamily nucleases are renowned for binding one divalent metal ion and requiring a conserved histidine to promote catalysis.
source: The histidine-metal (His-Me) superfamily nucleases are renowned for binding one divalent metal ion and requiring a conserved histidine to promote catalysis.
evidence: This is a characterization of His-Me nucleases based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Many His-Me family nucleases, including homing endonucleases and Cas9 nuclease, have been adapted for biotechnological and biomedical applications.
source: Many His-Me family nucleases, including homing endonucleases and Cas9 nuclease, have been adapted for biotechnological and biomedical applications.
evidence: This statement is supported by general knowledge about the applications of these nucleases.

claim: It remains unclear how the single metal ion in His-Me nucleases, together with the histidine, promotes water deprotonation, nucleophilic attack, and phosphodiester bond breakage.
source: However, it remains unclear how the single metal ion in His-Me nucleases, together with the histidine, promotes water deprotonation, nucleophilic attack, and phosphodiester bond breakage.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Only one divalent metal ion is required during I-PpoI catalysis.
source: By observing DNA hydrolysis in crystallo with His-Me I-PpoI nuclease as a model system, we proved that only one divalent metal ion is required during its catalysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from in crystallo observations.

claim: Several possible deprotonation pathways for the nucleophilic water were uncovered.
source: Moreover, we uncovered several possible deprotonation pathways for the nucleophilic water.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mutagenesis and structural data.

claim: Binding of the single metal ion and water deprotonation are concerted during catalysis.
source: Interestingly, binding of the single metal ion and water deprotonation are concerted during catalysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by pH-dependent experiments and structural observations.

claim: The catalytic mechanism of His-Me nucleases is distinct from multi-metal-ion-dependent DNA polymerases and nucleases.
source: Our results reveal catalytic details of His-Me nucleases, which is distinct from multi-metal-ion-dependent DNA polymerases and nucleases.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental findings and comparison with other enzyme systems.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases play fundamental roles in DNA replication and repair.
source: Mg2+-dependent nucleases play fundamental roles in DNA replication and repair (Kao and Bambara, 2003; Shen et al., 2005; Marti and Fleck, 2004; Mimitou and Symington, 2009), RNA processing (Patel and Steitz, 2003; Abelson et al., 1998; Chu and Rana, 2007; Moore and Proudfoot, 2009), as well as immune response and defense (James et al., 1996; Sorek et al., 2008; Tock and Dryden, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases are widely employed for genome editing in biotechnological and biomedical applications.
source: Moreover, they are widely employed for genome editing in biotechnological and biomedical applications (Adli, 2018; Carroll, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on genome editing applications.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases are proposed to cleave DNA through a SN2-type reaction.
source: These nucleases are proposed to cleave DNA through a SN2-type reaction, in which a water molecule, or sometimes, a tyrosine side chain (Grindley et al., 2006), initiates the nucleophilic attack on the scissile phosphate with the help of metal ions (Yang, 2011).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Metal ions can orient and stabilize the binding of the negatively charged nucleic acid backbone.
source: Metal ions can orient and stabilize the binding of the negatively charged nucleic acid backbone (Chen et al., 2017), promoting proton transfer, nucleophilic attack, and stabilization of the transition state.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases can be broadly categorized by the number of metal ions captured in their active site.
source: As a highly varied family of enzymes, Mg2+-dependent nucleases can be broadly categorized by the number of metal ions captured in their active site.
evidence: This is a classification based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mg2+-dependent nucleases with one and two metal ions have been observed.
source: So far, Mg2+-dependent nucleases with one and two metal ions have been observed.
evidence: This is based on prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: In two-Mg2+-ion-dependent nucleases, a metal ion binds on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate (Me2+B) while the other binds on the nucleophile side (Me2+A).
source: In the two-Mg2+-ion-dependent nuclease, a metal ion binds on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate (Me2+B) while the other binds on the nucleophile side (Me2+A).
evidence: This describes the metal ion binding configuration in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases, based on prior structural studies.

claim: In one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases, only the metal ion corresponding to the B site in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases is present.
source: In one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases, only the metal ion corresponding to the B site in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases is present (Yang, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Transiently bound metal ions have been identified in RNaseH and EndoV nucleases via time-resolved X-ray crystallography.
source: Moreover, transiently bound metal ions have been identified in the previously thought two-metal-ion RNaseH (Samara and Yang, 2018) and EndoV nucleases (Wu et al., 2019) via time-resolved X-ray crystallography, proposed to play key roles in various stages of their catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior time-resolved crystallography studies.

claim: Catalysis in the one-metal-ion-dependent APE1 nuclease has been observed in crystallo.
source: Similarly, catalysis in the one-metal-ion-dependent APE1 nuclease has been observed in crystallo, but mechanistic details regarding its metal-ion dependence have not been thoroughly explored (Freudenthal et al., 2015; Whitaker et al., 2018; Dupureur, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior crystallographic studies.

claim: Three-Zn2+-dependent nucleases exist, with two Zn2+ binding in the A- and B-equivalent positions, while the third Zn2+ coordinates the sp oxygen on the nucleophile side of the scissile phosphate.
source: There also exist three-Zn2+-dependent nucleases, with two Zn2+ binding in the A- and B-equivalent positions, while the third Zn2+ coordinating the sp oxygen on the nucleophile side of the scissile phosphate (Garcin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: It remains unclear how the single metal ion in one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases is capable of aligning the substrate, promoting deprotonation and nucleophilic attack, and stabilizing the pentacovalent transition state.
source: However, it remains unclear how the single metal ion in one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases is capable of aligning the substrate, promoting deprotonation and nucleophilic attack, and stabilizing the pentacovalent transition state.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: His-Me nucleases perform critical tasks in biological pathways such as apoptosis, extracellular defense, intracellular immunity (CRISPR–Cas9), and intron homing (homing endonuclease).
source: A large subfamily of one-metal-ion-dependent nucleases consist of histidine-metal (His-Me) nucleases that perform critical tasks in biological pathways such as apoptosis (Arnoult et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2016), extracellular defense (Cheng et al., 2002; Hsia et al., 2004), intracellular immunity (CRISPR–Cas9) (Doudna and Charpentier, 2014; Ran et al., 2013), and intron homing (homing endonuclease) (Chevalier and Stoddard, 2001; Stoddard, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The structural cores and active sites of His-Me nucleases are highly conserved despite sharing poor sequence homology.
source: Despite sharing poor sequence homology, the structural cores and active sites of His-Me nucleases are highly conserved and thus are proposed to catalyze DNA hydrolysis through a similar mechanism (Yang, 2011; Stoddard, 2005; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural and mechanistic studies.

claim: His-Me nucleases active sites all contain a single metal ion, a histidine, and an asparagine.
source: Surrounded by two beta sheets and an alpha helix, the His-Me nucleases active sites all contain a single metal ion, a histidine, and an asparagine (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figures.

claim: The asparagine residue helps to stabilize metal ion binding in His-Me nucleases.
source: The asparagine residue helps to stabilize metal ion binding whereas the strictly conserved histidine is suggested to deprotonate a nearby water for nucleophilic attack toward the scissile phosphate (Galburt et al., 1999; Pommer et al., 2001; Li et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The strictly conserved histidine is suggested to deprotonate a nearby water for nucleophilic attack toward the scissile phosphate.
source: The asparagine residue helps to stabilize metal ion binding whereas the strictly conserved histidine is suggested to deprotonate a nearby water for nucleophilic attack toward the scissile phosphate (Galburt et al., 1999; Pommer et al., 2001; Li et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The dynamic reaction process of DNA hydrolysis by His-Me nucleases has never been visualized.
source: To this day, the dynamic reaction process of DNA hydrolysis by His-Me nucleases has never been visualized, and the mechanism of single metal-ion-dependent and histidine-promoted catalysis remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Emerging genome editing and disease treatment involving CRISPR–Cas9 emphasize the importance of understanding the catalytic mechanism of DNA hydrolysis by His-Me nucleases.
source: Emerging genome editing and disease treatment involving CRISPR–Cas9 emphasize the importance of understanding the catalytic mechanism of DNA hydrolysis by His-Me nucleases (Schwank et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on CRISPR-Cas9 applications.

claim: Recent crystal and cryo-electron microscope structures of Cas9 have captured the His-Me family Cas9 histidine–asparagine–histidine (HNH) active site engaged with DNA before and after cleavage.
source: Recent crystal and cryo-electron microscope structures of Cas9 have captured the His-Me family Cas9 histidine–asparagine–histidine (HNH) active site engaged with DNA before and after cleavage (Sun et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2019; Das et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: Key catalytic details of Cas9, such as metal ion dependence, transition-state stabilization, and alternative deprotonation pathways, remain elusive due to relatively low resolution and the static nature of the structures.
source: However, due to the relatively low resolution and the static nature of the structures, key catalytic details, such as metal ion dependence, transition-state stabilization, and alternative deprotonation pathways, remain elusive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of prior structural studies.

claim: The large size and multiple conformational checkpoints during Cas9 catalysis hinder in crystallo observation of Cas9 catalysis.
source: Moreover, the large size and multiple conformational checkpoints during Cas9 catalysis (Sun et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2019; Das et al., 2023) hinder in crystallo observation of Cas9 catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies of Cas9.

claim: A dimer of I-PpoI was found in the asymmetric unit, with both active sites engaged for catalysis and DNA in the middle bent by 55°.
source: Similar to previous studies, a dimer of I-PpoI was found in the asymmetric unit, with both active sites engaged for catalysis and DNA in the middle bent by 55° (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: The two I-PpoI molecules in the asymmetric unit were almost identical and served as internal controls for evaluating the reaction process.
source: The two I-PpoI molecules were almost identical and thus served as internal controls for evaluating the reaction process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: Within each I-PpoI active site, a water molecule (nucleophilic water, WatN) existed 3.6 Å from the scissile phosphate, near the imidazole side chain of His98.
source: Within each I-PpoI active site, a water molecule (nucleophilic water, WatN) existed 3.6 Å from the scissile phosphate, near the imidazole side chain of His98.
evidence: This is based on structural data from the crystal structure.

claim: On the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate, the metal exhibited an octahedral geometry, being coordinated by three water molecules, two oxygen atoms from the scissile phosphate, and the conserved asparagine.
source: On the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate, the metal exhibited an octahedral geometry, being coordinated by three water molecules, two oxygen atoms from the scissile phosphate, and the conserved asparagine (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: Malonate in the crystallization buffer may chelate metal ions and hinder metal ion diffusion.
source: Next, we removed malonate in the crystallization buffer, which may chelate metal ions and hinder metal ion diffusion (Deerfield et al., 1991), by equilibrating the crystals in 200 mM NaCl buffer at pH 6, 7, or 8 for 30 min.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on malonate's chelating properties.

claim: The diffraction quality of the crystals was not affected during the soaking.
source: The diffraction quality of the crystals was not affected during the soaking.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: The structures of I-PpoI equilibrated at pH 6, 7, or 8 in the presence of 200 mM NaCl showed no signs of product formation and appeared similar to the malonate and previous reported I-PpoI structures.
source: The structures of I-PpoI equilibrated at pH 6, 7, or 8 in the presence of 200 mM NaCl showed no signs of product formation and appeared similar to the malonate and previous reported I-PpoI structures (Galburt et al., 1999; Flick et al., 1998; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure and comparison with prior structures.

claim: Tl+ anomalous electron density was detected at the metal ion-binding site without product formation after soaking I-PpoI crystals in buffer containing Tl+.
source: To confirm if a monovalent metal ion binds in the pre-reaction state, we soaked the I-PpoI crystals in buffer containing Tl+ and detected anomalous electron density at the metal ion-binding site without product formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: Monovalent metal ion can bind within the active site without initiating reaction.
source: Our results support that the monovalent metal ion can bind within the active site without initiating reaction, in corroboration with our biochemical assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data.

claim: After 600 s soaking in 500 µM Mg2+, a significant negative Fo − Fc peak on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate atom as well as a positive Fo − Fc peak on the other side were observed, indicating that DNA hydrolysis was occurring in crystallo.
source: After 600 s soaking, we saw a significant negative Fo − Fc peak on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate atom as well as a positive Fo − Fc peak on the other side (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), indicating that DNA hydrolysis was occurring in crystallo.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: After DNA cleavage, the newly generated phosphate group shifted 1 Å toward the WatN.
source: After DNA cleavage, the newly generated phosphate group shifted 1 Å toward the WatN (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: An additional product state was observed after soaking the crystals in 500 µM Mg2+ for 600 and 1800 s, at which the newly formed phosphate shifted 3 Å away from the metal ion to form a hydrogen bond with Arg61.
source: Furthermore, an additional product state was observed after soaking the crystals in 500 µM Mg2+ for 600 and 1800 s, at which the newly formed phosphate shifted 3 Å away from the metal ion to form a hydrogen bond with Arg61 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: Density between the reactant phosphate and nucleophilic water increased along with longer soaking time, indicating the generation of phosphate products.
source: Density between the reactant phosphate and nucleophilic water increased along with longer soaking time, indicating the generation of phosphate products (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: During the reaction, the coordination distances of the metal ion ligands decreased 0.1–0.2 Å when Mg2+ exchanged with Na+, which is consistent with their preferred geometry.
source: During the reaction, the coordination distances of the metal ion ligands decreased 0.1–0.2 Å when Mg2+ exchanged with Na+, which is consistent with their preferred geometry (Cowan, 2002; Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure and a citation to prior research on metal ion coordination geometry.

claim: At reaction time 160 s, 45% of product had been generated, which later plateaued to 65% at 300 s.
source: At reaction time 160 s, 45% of product had been generated (Figure 2D), which later plateaued to 65% at 300 s.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of structural data shown in the figure.

claim: During the reaction process, the sugar ring of the reactant and product DNA that resides around 3 Å away from the scissile phosphate, remained in a C3′-endo conformation.
source: During the reaction process, the sugar ring of the reactant and product DNA that resides around 3 Å away from the scissile phosphate, remained in a C3′-endo conformation.
evidence: This is based on structural data from the crystal structures.

claim: As Mg2+ soaking time increased from 10 to 160 s, the WatN was observed approaching the scissile phosphate.
source: As Mg2+ soaking time increased from 10 to 160 s, we observed the WatN approaching the scissile phosphate (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: The conserved His98 sidechain proposed to deprotonate the WatN was slightly rotated as Mg2+ soaking time increased.
source: At the same time, the conserved His98 sidechain proposed to deprotonate the WatN was slightly rotated.
evidence: This is based on structural data from the crystal structures.

claim: The electron density for the Mg2+ metal ion strongly correlated (R2 = 0.97) with product formation throughout the reaction process with Mg2+.
source: Throughout the reaction process with Mg2+, we found that the electron density for the Mg2+ metal ion strongly correlated (R2 = 0.97) with product formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C), which may suggest that saturation of this metal ion site is required and sufficient for catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of structural data shown in the figure.

claim: Saturation of the Mg2+ metal ion site may be required and sufficient for catalysis.
source: Throughout the reaction process with Mg2+, we found that the electron density for the Mg2+ metal ion strongly correlated (R2 = 0.97) with product formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, C), which may suggest that saturation of this metal ion site is required and sufficient for catalysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strong correlation between metal ion binding and product formation.

claim: With 500 µM Mn2+ in the reaction buffer, the reaction process and the product conformation were similar to that for Mg2+.
source: With 500 µM Mn2+ in the reaction buffer, we found that the reaction process and the product conformation were similar to that for Mg2+.
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural data from Mg2+ and Mn2+ soaking experiments.

claim: After 160 s Mn2+ soaking, clear anomalous signal was present at the metal ion-binding site, confirming the binding of Mn2+.
source: After 160 s Mn2+ soaking, clear anomalous signal was present at the metal ion-binding site, confirming the binding of Mn2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: For crystal structures of I-PpoI with partial product formation, Mn2+ signal at the metal ion site correlated with product formation with a R2 of 0.98.
source: For crystal structures of I-PpoI with partial product formation, Mn2+ signal at the metal ion site correlated with product formation with a R2 of 0.98 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of structural data shown in the figure.

claim: Apart from the single metal ion-binding site, no anomalous signal for additional Mn2+ was detected after soaking I-PpoI crystals in 200 mM Mn2+ for 600 s, at which 80% product formed within the active site.
source: However, apart from the single metal ion-binding site, we do not detect anomalous signal for additional Mn2+, despite such high concentration of Mn2+ (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: The strong correlation between product phosphate formation with Mn2+ binding and the absence of additional anomalous density peaks in heavy Mn2+ soaked crystals suggest that one and only one divalent metal ion is involved in I-PpoI DNA hydrolysis.
source: The strong correlation between product phosphate formation with Mn2+ binding and the absence of additional anomalous density peaks in heavy Mn2+ soaked crystals suggest that one and only one divalent metal ion is involved in I-PpoI DNA hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data on Mn2+ binding and product formation.

claim: Product conversion remained unaffected with increasing Tl+ in solution, apart from precipitation that occurred at 50 and 100 mM Tl+.
source: Apart from precipitation that occurred at 50 and 100 mM Tl+, we found that product conversion remained unaffected with increasing Tl+ in solution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure.

claim: Increasing Na+ concentration in solution did not increase product conversion.
source: Similarly, increasing Na+ concentration in solution did not increase product conversion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure.

claim: Only one Tl+ was detected by its anomalous signal in the pre-reaction state.
source: In addition, only one Tl+ was detected by its anomalous signal in the pre-reaction state (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: The biochemical and structural results indicate that additional monovalent metal ion may not be necessary for DNA hydrolysis.
source: The biochemical and structural results indicate that additional monovalent metal ion may not be necessary for DNA hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical and structural data.

claim: I-PpoI cleavage activity increased with pH with a pKa of 8.3.
source: The DNA cleavage assay revealed that I-PpoI cleavage activity increased with pH with a pKa of 8.3 (Figure 4A), which is much higher than the pKa of histidine, but the histidine pKa and the proton transfer process may be affected by the active site environment.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure.

claim: The pKa of 8.3 for I-PpoI cleavage activity is much higher than the pKa of histidine, but the histidine pKa and the proton transfer process may be affected by the active site environment.
source: The DNA cleavage assay revealed that I-PpoI cleavage activity increased with pH with a pKa of 8.3 (Figure 4A), which is much higher than the pKa of histidine, but the histidine pKa and the proton transfer process may be affected by the active site environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pKa and knowledge of histidine pKa.

claim: Higher pH resulted in faster product formation in crystallo, consistent with in solution experiments.
source: Consistent with in solution experiments, higher pH resulted in faster product formation in crystallo (Figure 4B), indicating that metal ion binding may also be affected by pH.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: Metal ion binding may be affected by pH.
source: Consistent with in solution experiments, higher pH resulted in faster product formation in crystallo (Figure 4B), indicating that metal ion binding may also be affected by pH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH-dependent product formation.

claim: Over 100 times higher concentration of Mg2+ was needed to yield 50% product in pH 6 versus 8.
source: Our results showed that over 100 times higher concentration of Mg2+ was needed to yield 50% product in pH 6 versus 8 (Figure 4C), confirming that pH affects metal-ion-dependent I-PpoI catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure.

claim: pH affects metal-ion-dependent I-PpoI catalysis.
source: Our results showed that over 100 times higher concentration of Mg2+ was needed to yield 50% product in pH 6 versus 8 (Figure 4C), confirming that pH affects metal-ion-dependent I-PpoI catalysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical assay data.

claim: The reactions in crystallo at higher pH reached 50% product formation at shorter soaking times (320 s at pH 6, 160 s at pH 7, and 80 s at pH 8, respectively).
source: Likewise, the reactions in crystallo at higher pH reached 50% product formation at shorter soaking times (320 s at pH 6, 160 s at pH 7, and 80 s at pH 8, respectively).
evidence: This is based on quantification of structural data from in crystallo experiments.

claim: The crystal structures that contained 30–35% product at pH 6 and 8 were nearly identical.
source: Interestingly, the crystal structures that contained 30–35% product at pH 6 and 8 were nearly identical (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: The positions of the His98 residue and the WatN were practically superimposable at pH 6 and 8.
source: The positions of the His98 residue and the WatN were practically superimposable (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: At all pH, Mg2+ binding strongly correlated with product formation (R2 > 0.95), suggesting that low pH reduces the overall reaction rate without altering the reaction pathway.
source: At all pH, Mg2+ binding strongly correlated with product formation (R2 > 0.95), suggesting that low pH reduces the overall reaction rate without altering the reaction pathway (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data at different pH values.

claim: H98A I-PpoI displayed residual activity but required a reaction time of 1 hr to be comparable to WT I-PpoI.
source: Our assays showed that H98A I-PpoI displayed residual activity but required a reaction time of 1 hr to be comparable to WT I-PpoI (Figure 5B), similar to the H98Q mutant in previous studies (Eastberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure and comparison with prior studies.

claim: Varying the pH resulted in a sigmoidal activity curve of H98A I-PpoI pH dependence, corresponding to a pKa of 7.9.
source: Furthermore, varying the pH resulted in a sigmoidal activity curve of I-PpoI pH dependence, corresponding to a pKa of 7.9 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure.

claim: The significantly reduced reaction rate and the shift of pH dependence suggest that His98 plays a key role in pH sensing and water deprotonation.
source: The significantly reduced reaction rate and the shift of pH dependence suggest that His98 plays a key role in pH sensing and water deprotonation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical assay data on H98A mutant.

claim: The low but existing activity of H98A I-PpoI suggests the presence of alternative general bases for proton transfer.
source: On the other hand, the low but existing activity of H98A I-PpoI suggests the presence of alternative general bases for proton transfer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the residual activity of H98A mutant.

claim: His78 resides on the nucleophile side 3.8 Å from the WatN, with a cluster of water molecules in between.
source: Another histidine (His78) resides on the nucleophile side 3.8 Å from the WatN, with a cluster of water molecules in between (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: The single mutant, H78A I-PpoI, had an activity similar to WT.
source: The DNA cleavage assays revealed that the single mutant, H78A I-PpoI, had an activity similar to WT, whereas the double mutant (H78A/H98A I-PpoI) exhibited much lower activity than that of H98A (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure.

claim: The double mutant (H78A/H98A I-PpoI) exhibited much lower activity than that of H98A.
source: The DNA cleavage assays revealed that the single mutant, H78A I-PpoI, had an activity similar to WT, whereas the double mutant (H78A/H98A I-PpoI) exhibited much lower activity than that of H98A (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure.

claim: Varying the pH for H78A/H98A I-PpoI resulted in a sigmoidal activity curve that corresponded to a pKa of 8.7.
source: Furthermore, varying the pH for H78A/H98A I-PpoI resulted in a sigmoidal activity curve that corresponded to a pKa of 8.7 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure.

claim: The results confirm the possibility of His78 as an alternative general base.
source: In consistent with previous speculations, our results confirm the possibility of His78 as an alternative general base (Eastberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical assay data on H78A and H78A/H98A mutants, supported by a citation to prior speculation.

claim: The residual activity and pH dependence of H78A/H98A I-PpoI indicated that something else was still activating the nucleophilic water in the absence of any nearby histidine.
source: The residual activity and pH dependence of H78A/H98A I-PpoI indicated that something else was still activating the nucleophilic water in the absence of any nearby histidine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the residual activity of the double mutant.

claim: Titrating imidazole in H98A and H78A/H98A I-PpoI partially rescued cleavage activity.
source: Furthermore, we found that titrating imidazole in H98A and H78A/H98A I-PpoI partially rescued cleavage activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B), similar as observed in Cas9 and EndA nuclease (Furuhata and Kato, 2021; Moon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assay data shown in the figure and comparison with prior studies.

claim: His98 is the primary proton acceptor like previous simulation results.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that His98 is the primary proton acceptor like previous simulation results (Maghsoud et al., 2023) but at the same time, I-PpoI can use alternative pathways to activate the nucleophilic WatN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and biochemical data, supported by a citation to prior simulation results.

claim: I-PpoI can use alternative pathways to activate the nucleophilic WatN.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that His98 is the primary proton acceptor like previous simulation results (Maghsoud et al., 2023) but at the same time, I-PpoI can use alternative pathways to activate the nucleophilic WatN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and biochemical data.

claim: The metal ion was not observed in crystallo when His98 was removed, even after soaking in 1 mM Mn2+.
source: To confirm divalent metal ion binding, the H98A I-PpoI crystals were soaked for 1800s in 500 µM Mn2+, the same concentration used to initiate DNA hydrolysis by WT I-PpoI. However, to our surprise, the metal ion-binding site was devoid of any anomalous signal. Increasing the Mn2+ concentration to 1 mM still did not produce anomalous density at the Me2+-binding site (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in the figure.

claim: Metal ion binding can be altered by perturbing His98 and possibly water deprotonation, even though the metal ion-binding site and His98 exist 7 Å apart without direct interaction.
source: The results indicate that metal ion binding can be altered by perturbing His98 and possibly water deprotonation, even though the metal ion-binding site and His98 exist 7 Å apart without direct interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data on H98A mutant.

claim: Perturbing the deprotonation pathway not only affects nucleophilic attack but also metal binding.
source: Our results indicate that perturbing the deprotonation pathway not only affects nucleophilic attack but also metal binding, suggesting that I-PpoI catalyzes DNA catalysis via a concerted mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data on H98A mutant.

claim: I-PpoI catalyzes DNA catalysis via a concerted mechanism.
source: Our results indicate that perturbing the deprotonation pathway not only affects nucleophilic attack but also metal binding, suggesting that I-PpoI catalyzes DNA catalysis via a concerted mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Time-resolved crystallography can visualize time-dependent structural changes and elucidate mechanisms of enzyme catalysis with unparalleled detail in crystallo.
source: Time-resolved crystallography can visualize time-dependent structural changes and elucidate mechanisms of enzyme catalysis with unparalleled detail in crystallo, especially for light-dependent enzymes, in which the reactions can be synchronously initiated by light pulses (Wilson, 2022; Brändén and Neutze, 2021; Maestre-Reyna et al., 2023; Christou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on time-resolved crystallography.

claim: Metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallographic techniques have uncovered rich dynamics at the active site and transient metal ion binding during the catalytic processes of metal-ion-dependent DNA polymerases, nucleases, and glycosylase.
source: In complementary, recently advanced metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallographic techniques have uncovered rich dynamics at the active site and transient metal ion binding during the catalytic processes of metal-ion-dependent DNA polymerases (Freudenthal et al., 2013; Gao and Yang, 2016; Nakamura et al., 2012; Vyas et al., 2015; Chim et al., 2021; Gregory et al., 2021), nucleases (Samara and Yang, 2018; Wu et al., 2019), and glycosylase (Demir et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research using metal ion diffusion-based time-resolved crystallography.

claim: Transient metal ions have been shown to play critical roles in catalysis, such as water deprotonation for nucleophilic attack in RNaseH, bond breakage and product stabilization in polymerases, and alignment of the substrate and nucleophilic water in MutT.
source: In addition to metal ions captured in static structures, these transient metal ions have been shown to play critical roles in catalysis, such as water deprotonation for nucleophilic attack in RNaseH (Samara and Yang, 2018), bond breakage and product stabilization in polymerases (Freudenthal et al., 2013; Gao and Yang, 2016; Nakamura et al., 2012; Vyas et al., 2015; Gregory et al., 2021; Reed and Suo, 2017; Chang et al., 2022), and alignment of the substrate and nucleophilic water in MutT (Nakamura and Yamagata, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on transient metal ions.

claim: The observed location of the Me2+ on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate corresponds to the Me2+B in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases.
source: The observed location of the Me2+ on the leaving group side of the scissile phosphate corresponds to the Me2+B in two-metal-ion-dependent nucleases (Yang, 2008; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and comparison with prior research.

claim: The metal ion in I-PpoI is coordinated by a water cluster and asparagine side chain rather than the acidic aspartate and glutamic acid clusters that outline the active sites of RNaseH and APE1 nuclease as well as DNA polymerases.
source: First, it is coordinated by a water cluster and asparagine side chain (sometimes with an additional aspartate residue) rather than the acidic aspartate and glutamic acid clusters that outline the active sites of RNaseH and APE1 nuclease (Tsutakawa et al., 2013) as well as DNA polymerases (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and comparison with prior structures.

claim: Even in the absence of divalent Mg2+ or Mn2+, the active site including the scissile phosphate was already well aligned in I-PpoI, which is different from RNaseH.
source: Even in the absence of divalent Mg2+ or Mn2+, the active site including the scissile phosphate was already well aligned in I-PpoI, which is again different from RNaseH.
evidence: This is based on structural data from the pre-reaction state.

claim: Leu116 and the beta sheet consisting of Arg61, Gln63, Lys65, and Thr67 helped to position the DNA optimally toward the active site.
source: Instead, Leu116 and the beta sheet consisting of Arg61, Gln63, Lys65, and Thr67 (Flick et al., 1998; Galburt et al., 2000) helped to position the DNA optimally toward the active site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and citations to prior research.

claim: Single metal ion binding is strictly correlated with product formation in all conditions, at different pH and with different mutants.
source: Second, single metal ion binding is strictly correlated with product formation in all conditions, at different pH and with different mutants (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E; Moon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and citations to prior research.

claim: Similar to the third metal ion in DNA polymerases and RNaseH, the metal ion in I-PpoI is not required for substrate alignment but is essential for catalysis.
source: Thus, similar to the third metal ion in DNA polymerases and RNaseH, the metal ion in I-PpoI is not required for substrate alignment but is essential for catalysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data and comparison with other enzyme systems.

claim: The single metal ion helps stabilize the transition state and reduce the electronegative buildup of DNA, thereby promoting DNA hydrolysis.
source: We suspect that the single metal ion helps stabilize the transition state and reduce the electronegative buildup of DNA, thereby promoting DNA hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the role of the metal ion in catalysis.

claim: His98 is perfectly positioned to mediate the proton transfer, existing close to the nucleophilic water at 2.6 Å.
source: Existing close to the nucleophilic water at 2.6 Å, His98 is perfectly positioned to mediate the proton transfer.
evidence: This is based on structural data from the crystal structure.

claim: Due to the bulky presence of His98 and beta sheet protein residues, there is no space for an additional metal ion at the nucleophilic side.
source: Moreover, due to the bulky presence of His98 and beta sheet protein residues, there is no space for an additional metal ion at the nucleophilic side (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on structural data shown in the figure.

claim: His78, imidazole, or its surrounding waters may serve as alternative general bases for accepting the proton, similar to Pol η.
source: But since H98A I-PpoI showed residual activity, His78, imidazole, or its surrounding waters may still serve as alternative general bases for accepting the proton, similar to Pol η, in which primer 3′-OH deprotonation can occur through multiple pathways (Gregory et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the residual activity of H98A mutant and comparison with prior research.

claim: Water deprotonation and metal ion binding appeared to be highly correlated based on in crystallo observations.
source: Based on our in crystallo observations, water deprotonation and metal ion binding appeared to be highly correlated (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data.

claim: Lowering the pH not only reduced reaction rate but also slowed metal ion binding.
source: Lowering the pH not only reduced reaction rate but also slowed metal ion binding (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data shown in the figure.

claim: The divalent metal ion may be sensitive to the charge potential of the substrate scissile phosphate, which may be indirectly affected by the deprotonated state of the nucleophilic water.
source: As there is no direct interaction between His98 and the Me2+-binding site, the divalent metal ion may be sensitive to the charge potential of the substrate scissile phosphate, which may be indirectly affected by the deprotonated state of the nucleophilic water.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed correlation between pH, metal ion binding, and product formation.

claim: Binding of the divalent metal ion may alter the local electrostatic environment and affect His98 deprotonation.
source: Conversely, binding of the divalent metal ion may alter the local electrostatic environment and affect His98 deprotonation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed correlation between metal ion binding and product formation.

claim: Previous molecular dynamics simulation of Cas9 has suggested that the histidine pKa is highly sensitive to active site changes.
source: Consistently, previous molecular dynamics simulation of Cas9 has suggested that the histidine pKa is highly sensitive to active site changes (Nierzwicki et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior simulation research.

claim: Without a proper proton acceptor, the metal ion may be prone for dissociation without the reaction proceeding, and thus stable Mg2+ binding was not observed in crystallo without His98.
source: Without a proper proton acceptor, the metal ion may be prone for dissociation without the reaction proceeding, and thus stable Mg2+ binding was not observed in crystallo without His98 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data on H98A mutant.

claim: Optimal alignment of the metal ion and WatN within the active site, labeled as metal-binding state, leads to irreversible bond breakage.
source: On the other hand, optimal alignment of the metal ion and WatN within the active site, labeled as metal-binding state, leads to irreversible bond breakage (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural data.

claim: The experimental observations suggest a concerted mechanism for one-metal-ion promoted DNA hydrolysis.
source: In summary, our experimental observations suggest a concerted mechanism for one-metal-ion promoted DNA hydrolysis, offering guidance for future computational analysis of enzyme catalysis (Nierzwicki et al., 2022) and the rational design and engineering of nucleases (Ashworth et al., 2006) for biotechnological and biomedical applications.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
